fieldMarks: Stocky, short-legged animal with a slight shoulder hump, very short tail and long guard hair hanging nearly to the ground.
Dark brown coat with creamy hair on the saddle, forehead and legs.
Both sexes have horns that curve down beside the face and up at the tips; on bulls the bases form a solid boss across the forehead, while cows have a fur patch between the horn bases.
Bulls about 5 ft at the shoulder and 600-800 lb (Alaska data); cows smaller.
In midsummer the woolly undercoat (qiviut) sheds, leaving animals shaggy and ragged for weeks.
behavior: Winter herds may hold up to 75 animals; herds break into small groups around calving.
Rut August-October: bulls give deep, rumbling roar-like bellows and charge head-on, clashing horn bosses repeatedly.
Eats grasses, sedges, forbs and woody plants; poorly adapted to digging through heavy snow, so winter range is limited to areas of shallow snow.
Endures severe storms lying down with its back to the wind.
habitat: Low-lying coastal and inland plains and river valleys of the Arctic where shrubs are most abundant.
range: Native populations in North America occur only in northern Canada, mostly on the Arctic islands (especially Banks and Victoria), with a mainland population north of Great Bear Lake, around Queen Maud Gulf and in northeastern Keewatin. Introduced free-ranging population in Quebec; reintroduced to Alaska from Greenland stock in 1930 (Nunivak Island, later Seward Peninsula and elsewhere).
